subject: Physics
title: Nuclei
summary: What sits inside the nucleus, how big and how dense it is, why its mass is less than the sum of its parts, the nuclear force that holds it together, and how fission and fusion release energy. A short, formula-light chapter where the binding-energy curve and a handful of numericals decide the marks.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit VIII (Atoms and Nuclei, Chapters 12 and 13) carries 7 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. Nuclei typically takes 3 to 4 of those: one 2-mark or 3-mark question (a radius or density numerical, a binding-energy calculation, or the binding-energy curve with its conclusions) plus a 1-mark MCQ or assertion-reason. In some years the binding-energy curve appears inside a 5-mark or case-based question shared with Atoms.

question_types.note: Ratio of nuclear radii from mass numbers; nuclear density being independent of A; the energy equivalent of 1 u; which nucleus has the highest binding energy per nucleon; energy released per fission of uranium; a property that is not true of the nuclear force; number of neutrons in a given nuclide.

Nuclear density same for all nuclei; energy release in fission linked to higher binding energy per nucleon of the fragments; nuclear force being charge independent or short range; fusion needing very high temperature because of Coulomb repulsion.

Find the radius of one nucleus from another; define mass defect and binding energy; state two properties of the nuclear force; a one-step energy calculation from given binding energies; explain why the daughter nucleus in fusion has higher binding energy per nucleon.

Show that nuclear density is independent of A; draw the potential energy versus separation curve for two nucleons and read off the regions; compute the binding energy of a nucleus from given masses; energy released when a heavy nucleus splits, using binding energy per nucleon values.

Draw the binding energy per nucleon versus mass number curve, state its features and use it to explain energy release in both fission and fusion; nuclear fusion in the Sun with the proton-proton chain and the temperature argument; a combined theory-plus-numerical question.
A passage on the binding-energy curve, on fission of uranium-235, or on fusion in stars, followed by four one-mark parts that test reading the curve, the sign of Q, and simple ratios.

hot_topics: Binding energy per nucleon versus mass number curve: features and the conclusions drawn from it
Energy release in fission and fusion explained from the curve
R = R<sub>0</sub>A<sup>1/3</sup>: radius ratios and the constancy of nuclear density
Mass defect and binding energy numericals using 1 u = 931.5 MeV
Properties of the nuclear force and the potential energy versus separation graph
Fission of uranium-235: the reaction, Q about 200 MeV, energy from 1 kg of fuel
Fusion in the Sun: proton-proton chain, 26.7 MeV, why a very high temperature is needed
Composition of the nucleus: isotopes, isobars, isotones, discovery of the neutron

sections.heading: 13.1 Introduction
sections.body:
Chapter 12 ended with Rutherford's picture: almost the whole mass of an atom, and all of its positive charge, sits in a nucleus about 10−14 m across, inside an atom about 10−10 m across. The nucleus is therefore roughly 104 times smaller in radius than the atom, so its volume is about 1012 times smaller. Nearly all the atom's mass is packed into that tiny volume, which already tells you the nucleus must be extraordinarily dense.

This chapter asks the next set of questions. What is the nucleus made of? How big is it, and does its size follow a rule? Why is the measured mass of a nucleus always less than the sum of the masses of its constituents, and what does that missing mass have to do with energy? What force holds positively charged protons together against their Coulomb repulsion? And finally, how do fission and fusion release energy on a scale that powers reactors and stars?

In the current rationalised syllabus the chapter has six parts: composition of the nucleus, its size, mass-energy and binding energy, the nuclear force, and nuclear energy through fission and fusion. Radioactivity (decay law, half-life, alpha, beta and gamma decay) and the nuclear reactor were removed from the CBSE syllabus in 2023-24, so board questions from before that year on half-life are no longer in scope. Almost every mark in this chapter is earned by understanding one graph, the binding energy per nucleon against mass number, and by being fluent with the conversion 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c2.
sections.tip: Keep the two scales in your head: atom about 10<sup>−10</sup> m, nucleus about 10<sup>−14</sup> to 10<sup>−15</sup> m. One-mark questions like to ask for the ratio of atomic to nuclear size (about 10<sup>4</sup>) or of their volumes (about 10<sup>12</sup>).

sections.heading: 13.2 Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus
sections.body:
Atomic mass unit. Atomic masses are tiny, so they are measured in the atomic mass unit u, defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom: 1 u = 1.660539 × 10−27 kg. Mass spectrometers measure atomic masses very precisely, and they show that most elements are mixtures of isotopes, atoms with the same atomic number but different masses. Chlorine, for example, has isotopes of masses 34.98 u (75.4%) and 36.98 u (24.6%); the weighted average, (75.4 × 34.98 + 24.6 × 36.98)/100 = 35.47 u, is the atomic mass you see in the periodic table. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (99.985%), deuterium (0.015%) and tritium (unstable, made artificially).

Constituents. The lightest hydrogen nucleus is the proton, with charge +e and mass mp = 1.00727 u = 1.67262 × 10−27 kg, about 1836 times the electron mass. The number of protons is the atomic number Z, and it fixes the element. Since deuterium and tritium have one proton each but roughly two and three times the mass, the nucleus must also contain neutral particles. Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles: 42He + 94Be → 126C + 10n. The neutron is neutral, with mn = 1.00866 u = 1.6749 × 10−27 kg, very slightly heavier than the proton. A free neutron is unstable (it decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino with a mean life of about 1000 s) but it is stable inside a nucleus.

Notation. A nuclide is written AZX where Z is the number of protons, N is the number of neutrons and A = Z + N is the mass number, the total number of nucleons. Gold-197 has Z = 79, so N = 118. The three families you must be able to name: isotopes have the same Z (1H, 2H, 3H); isobars have the same A (3H and 3He); isotones have the same N (198Hg and 197Au, both with 118 neutrons).

formulas.expr: 1 u = 1.660539 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg = 1/12 of the mass of a <sup>12</sup>C atom

sections.tip: Chemists' atomic masses (tables) are masses of neutral atoms, which include the electrons. NCERT numericals give atomic masses and use m(<sup>1</sup>H) = 1.007825 u, not m<sub>p</sub>, so the electron masses cancel. Use whichever the question gives; do not mix the two.

sections.heading: 13.3 Size of the Nucleus
sections.body:
Rutherford's alpha-scattering gave the first estimate of nuclear size. Later experiments that scattered fast electrons off many different nuclei showed a clean empirical rule: a nucleus of mass number A has radius

R = R0A1/3, with R0 = 1.2 × 10−15 m = 1.2 fm.

Radius grows only as the cube root of A, so volume, (4/3)πR3 = (4/3)πR03A, grows in direct proportion to A. Each nucleon takes up about the same volume no matter how large the nucleus. This is the fact behind the most common 3-mark derivation in the chapter.

Nuclear density is independent of A. Take the mass of the nucleus as A × m, where m is the average nucleon mass (about 1.67 × 10−27 kg, ignoring the small binding-energy correction). Then

ρ = mass/volume = A m / [(4/3)πR03A] = 3m / (4πR03).

A cancels, so every nucleus has the same density. Putting in the numbers: ρ = 3 × 1.67 × 10−27 / [4 × 3.14 × (1.2 × 10−15)3] = 5.01 × 10−27 / 2.17 × 10−44 ≈ 2.3 × 1017 kg m−3. Compare water at 103 kg m−3: nuclear matter is about 1014 times denser. This is why the atom is mostly empty space.

Radius ratios. Since R ∝ A1/3, R1/R2 = (A1/A2)1/3. The 2020 board question gave the radius of 27Al as 3.6 fm and asked for 64Cu: R = 3.6 × (64/27)1/3 = 3.6 × 4/3 = 4.8 fm. Examiners choose mass numbers that are perfect cubes or ratios of cubes (1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216), so look for that before reaching for a calculator.

where: mass of one nucleon, about 1.67 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg
mass numbers of the two nuclei

sections.tip: In the density derivation write 'mass = A m' and 'volume = (4/3)πR<sub>0</sub><sup>3</sup>A' as two separate lines before dividing. The marking scheme gives a mark for each, and a third for stating that A cancels so the density is independent of A.

sections.heading: 13.4.1 Mass-Energy
sections.body:
Before Einstein, mass and energy were conserved separately. In 1905 Einstein showed that mass is a form of energy, and that a mass m is equivalent to energy

E = mc2,

where c = 3 × 108 m s−1. The conversion factor c2 = 9 × 1016 m2 s−2 is enormous, which is why ordinary chemistry never notices the mass change. NCERT Example 13.2 makes the point: 1 g of any substance is equivalent to E = 10−3 × 9 × 1016 = 9 × 1013 J, a colossal amount of energy.

The consequence for physics is that the law of conservation of energy now includes mass. In a nuclear reaction the total mass of the products can differ from the total mass of the reactants, and the difference appears as kinetic energy, radiation, or is supplied from the kinetic energy of the incoming particles. So we speak of conservation of mass-energy, not of mass alone.

The number you will use constantly. The energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit is

E = 1.6605 × 10−27 × (2.9979 × 108)2 = 1.4924 × 10−10 J = 1.4924 × 10−10 / 1.602 × 10−19 eV = 931.5 × 106 eV.

So 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c2. Nuclear masses are therefore often quoted in MeV/c2, and a mass difference Δm in u converts to energy simply as Δm × 931.5 MeV. Every binding-energy and Q-value numerical in this chapter is a mass bookkeeping exercise followed by this one multiplication.

where: mass difference in atomic mass units

sections.tip: Write '1 u = 931.5 MeV' on the first line of any numerical that converts mass to energy. If the paper gives 931 or 932 MeV, use the paper's value, not your memorised one.

sections.heading: 13.4.2 Nuclear binding energy
sections.body:
Mass defect. The measured mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its free protons and neutrons. For oxygen-16: 8 protons + 8 neutrons = 8 × 1.00727 + 8 × 1.00866 = 16.12744 u, while the mass of the 16O nucleus (atomic mass 15.99493 u minus 8 electrons) is 15.99053 u. The difference, ΔM = 0.13691 u, is the mass defect. In general

ΔM = [Z mp + (A − Z) mn] − M.

Binding energy. By E = mc2, the mass defect is the energy that was released when the nucleons came together, and equally the energy you must supply to pull the nucleus apart into free nucleons: Eb = ΔM c2. For 16O, Eb = 0.13691 × 931.5 = 127.5 MeV. A more useful measure is the binding energy per nucleon, Ebn = Eb/A, the average energy needed to remove one nucleon; for 16O it is 127.5/16 = 7.97 MeV. The higher Ebn, the more stable the nucleus.

The curve. Plot Ebn against A for all stable nuclei and you get the most examined graph of the chapter. Its features: (i) Ebn is practically constant, close to 8 MeV, for 30 < A < 170, with a broad maximum of about 8.75 MeV at A = 56 (iron) and a value of 7.6 MeV at A = 238 (uranium); (ii) it is lower for light nuclei (A < 30) and falls slowly for heavy nuclei (A > 170); (iii) light nuclei such as 4He show small sharp peaks above the trend.

Conclusions the examiner wants. First, the force between nucleons is attractive and strong enough to bind by several MeV per nucleon. Second, the constancy of Ebn over the middle range shows the nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates: a nucleon interacts only with its few nearest neighbours, so adding more nucleons does not raise the energy per nucleon. For heavy nuclei the Coulomb repulsion, which is long-ranged and acts between all proton pairs, slowly lowers Ebn. Third, a heavy nucleus of A = 240 (Ebn ≈ 7.6 MeV) that splits into two fragments of A = 120 (Ebn ≈ 8.5 MeV) moves to more tightly bound products, so energy is released: this is fission. Fourth, two very light nuclei (A ≤ 10) that join to form a heavier one move up the steep left side of the curve, so energy is again released: this is fusion. In both cases the products are more tightly bound than the reactants and the difference in binding energy is released.

where: binding energy per nucleon; about 8.75 MeV at A = 56, 7.6 MeV at A = 238

sections.tip: When the question gives atomic masses (as in m(<sup>1</sup>H) = 1.007825 u) use Z m(<sup>1</sup>H) + N m<sub>n</sub> − m(atom); the electrons cancel. Never subtract electron masses on one side only. And label the axes of the curve: E<sub>bn</sub> in MeV on the y-axis, A on the x-axis, with Fe-56 marked at the peak.

sections.heading: 13.5 Nuclear Force
sections.body:
Protons packed into a few femtometres repel each other with Coulomb forces far larger than anything in chemistry, and the gravitational attraction between nucleons is hopelessly weak. A binding energy of about 8 MeV per nucleon needs a new force, the strong nuclear force. Its properties are read off the experiments and from the binding-energy curve:

  1. Strongest force known. It is much stronger than the Coulomb force and about 1038 times the gravitational force between two protons; otherwise no nucleus with more than one proton could exist.
  2. Short range and saturating. It falls to practically zero for separations beyond a few femtometres. Each nucleon therefore interacts only with its near neighbours, which is why Ebn is roughly constant from A = 30 to 170. The Coulomb force, in contrast, is long-ranged and is felt between every pair of protons.
  3. Attractive, then repulsive. The potential energy of a pair of nucleons plotted against their separation r has a minimum at r0 ≈ 0.8 fm. For r > r0 the force is attractive; for r < r0 it is strongly repulsive, which stops the nucleus collapsing. This graph is a regular 2- or 3-mark question.
  4. Charge independent. The n–n, p–p and n–p nuclear forces are very nearly equal; the force does not depend on electric charge.
  5. No simple law. Unlike Coulomb's inverse-square law there is no compact mathematical form; the force is described from experiment. It also depends on the relative spins of the nucleons, a point beyond this course.

When asked to 'draw the plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation', sketch a curve that is large and positive at very small r, crosses zero, drops to a minimum at about 0.8 fm, then rises back to zero and stays there beyond a few fm. Mark the attractive region (r > r0) and the repulsive region (r < r0), and write two features beside it: short range and charge independence.

formulas.expr: r<sub>0</sub> ≈ 0.8 fm at the minimum of the nucleon–nucleon potential energy

sections.tip: Students draw the potential-energy curve as a simple well and forget the steep repulsive wall at small r. The wall is what the examiner checks first, along with the label r<sub>0</sub> ≈ 0.8 fm.

sections.heading: 13.6.1 Nuclear Energy: Fission
sections.body:
The binding-energy curve says that a heavy nucleus can lower its energy by splitting, and a light pair can lower theirs by joining. Both processes release the binding-energy difference, and both are used as energy sources. Chemical reactions release a few eV per atom; nuclear reactions release a few MeV per nucleon, about a million times more per kilogram.

Fission was discovered in 1939 by Hahn and Strassmann. When a slow (thermal) neutron is absorbed by uranium-235 the compound nucleus 236U is highly excited and splits into two medium-mass fragments plus two or three fresh neutrons. One common channel:

10n + 23592U → 23692U → 14456Ba + 8936Kr + 3 10n

Other channels give 133Sb + 99Nb + 4n, or 140Xe + 94Sr + 2n. The fragments are themselves unstable and undergo further decays. Check the bookkeeping in any equation you write: Z and A must balance on both sides (92 = 56 + 36; 236 = 144 + 89 + 3).

Energy released. The parent has Ebn ≈ 7.6 MeV, the fragments about 8.5 MeV, so roughly 0.9 MeV per nucleon × 236 nucleons ≈ 200 MeV is released per fission. NCERT quotes Q ≈ 200 MeV. It appears first as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons and is then transferred to the surrounding matter as heat. One kilogram of 235U contains (1000/235) × 6.022 × 1023 ≈ 2.56 × 1024 nuclei, so complete fission of 1 kg gives 2.56 × 1024 × 200 × 1.6 × 10−13 J ≈ 8.2 × 1013 J.

Chain reaction. The two or three neutrons released can trigger further fissions. If on average more than one of them does, the number of fissions grows geometrically: uncontrolled, this is an atom bomb; controlled so that exactly one neutron per fission causes the next fission, it is a nuclear reactor, the source of nuclear electricity. The reactor's design (moderator, control rods, coolant) is no longer in the CBSE syllabus, but the one-line idea of the chain reaction still appears in case-based questions.

where: energy released per fission, about 200 MeV = 3.2 × 10<sup>−11</sup> J

formulas.expr: Energy released = (final total binding energy) − (initial total binding energy) = A<sub>1</sub>E<sub>bn1</sub> + A<sub>2</sub>E<sub>bn2</sub> − A E<sub>bn</sub>
where: mass number and binding energy per nucleon of the parent

sections.tip: Energy released = binding energy of products − binding energy of reactants. Students reverse the sign; remember that products are more tightly bound in an energy-releasing reaction, so their total binding energy is larger.

sections.heading: 13.6.2 Nuclear fusion: energy generation in stars
sections.body:
Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei into a heavier one. Because the product sits higher on the binding-energy curve, energy is released. Three deuterium reactions from NCERT:

11H + 11H → 21H + e+ + ν + 0.42 MeV
21H + 21H → 32He + n + 3.27 MeV
21H + 21H → 31H + 11H + 4.03 MeV

Why it is hard. Two nuclei must come within a few fm for the nuclear force to act, but until then they repel by the Coulomb force. The height of the barrier for two protons is about 400 keV, and higher for nuclei of larger charge. A gas whose particles have this much thermal energy on average, using (3/2)kT ≈ 400 keV, would be at about 3 × 109 K. Fusion is therefore called a thermonuclear reaction: it needs extreme temperature and pressure, which exist only in the interiors of stars. In practice the required temperature is lower than the crude estimate, because in a gas at a given temperature a fraction of particles has energies well above the average (the Maxwellian tail), and those are the ones that fuse. The Sun's core, at about 1.5 × 107 K, is hot enough.

The proton-proton chain. The Sun's energy comes from converting hydrogen to helium in these steps:

11H + 11H → 21H + e+ + ν + 0.42 MeV
e+ + e− → γ + γ + 1.02 MeV
21H + 11H → 32He + γ + 5.49 MeV
32He + 32He → 42He + 11H + 11H + 12.86 MeV

The first three steps occur twice for every fourth step. Adding everything up, the net reaction is

4 11H + 2 e− → 42He + 2ν + 6γ + 26.7 MeV.

Four hydrogen atoms become one helium atom with the release of 26.7 MeV. Helium is not further burnt while hydrogen lasts; the Sun has burnt hydrogen for about 5 × 109 years and has enough for about the same again. When the hydrogen runs out the core contracts, heats up, and helium begins to fuse into heavier elements, but that stage is beyond the syllabus.

formulas.expr: Coulomb barrier for two protons ≈ 400 keV; (3/2)kT ≈ K gives T ≈ 3 × 10<sup>9</sup> K; Sun's core ≈ 1.5 × 10<sup>7</sup> K

sections.tip: When asked why fusion needs a high temperature, say both halves: the nuclei must overcome Coulomb repulsion to come within the range of the nuclear force, and only thermal motion at very high temperature gives them that kinetic energy.

sections.heading: 13.6.3 Controlled thermonuclear fusion
sections.body:
Fission reactors work; fusion reactors do not yet exist commercially, and the reason is the temperature. The natural fusion process in the Sun is slow (the first proton-proton step has a very low probability), so a reactor would use faster reactions with deuterium and tritium, such as

21H + 31H → 42He + n + 17.59 MeV,

together with the deuterium-deuterium reactions releasing 3.27 MeV and 4.03 MeV. The fuel is attractive: deuterium is present in ordinary water, and the products are not long-lived radioactive waste.

To make the reaction go at a useful rate the fuel must be heated to about 108 K. At that temperature the gas is fully ionised, a plasma of bare nuclei and electrons, and no material container can hold it; contact with any wall would cool the plasma and destroy the wall. The central engineering problem is therefore confinement: holding a plasma at 108 K, at sufficient density, for long enough that fusion releases more energy than was spent heating it. Magnetic confinement (the tokamak) uses strong magnetic fields to keep charged particles away from the walls; inertial confinement compresses a fuel pellet with intense laser pulses. Large international projects are working on both, and the chapter notes that a practical fusion reactor is still some way off.

What the board can ask from this short section: the reaction and its Q value, why the temperature must be so high, why a plasma cannot be held in an ordinary vessel, and one advantage of fusion over fission as an energy source (abundant fuel, no long-lived radioactive fragments). Keep the answers to two or three lines each.
sections.tip: A 1-mark trap: 'Fusion is the source of energy in (a) nuclear reactor (b) atom bomb (c) the Sun (d) all of these.' Only the Sun. Present-day reactors and the atom bomb both use fission.

key_terms.definition: One-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; 1 u = 1.660539 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg, equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy.
A proton or a neutron, the two constituents of the nucleus.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element.
The total number of nucleons, A = Z + N.
Nuclides with the same Z but different A, e.g. <sup>1</sup>H, <sup>2</sup>H, <sup>3</sup>H; same chemistry, different mass.
Nuclides with the same mass number A but different Z, e.g. <sup>3</sup>H and <sup>3</sup>He.
Nuclides with the same number of neutrons N, e.g. <sup>197</sup>Au and <sup>198</sup>Hg (118 neutrons each).
R = R<sub>0</sub>A<sup>1/3</sup> with R<sub>0</sub> = 1.2 fm; the volume of a nucleus is proportional to its mass number.
Mass per unit volume of nuclear matter, about 2.3 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>, the same for all nuclei.
The difference between the sum of the masses of the free nucleons and the measured mass of the nucleus: ΔM = [Z m<sub>p</sub> + (A − Z) m<sub>n</sub>] − M.
The energy needed to separate a nucleus into its free nucleons, equal to the energy released when they bind: E<sub>b</sub> = ΔM c<sup>2</sup>.
E<sub>b</sub>/A, the average energy needed to remove one nucleon; a measure of nuclear stability, maximum about 8.75 MeV near A = 56.
The strong, short-range, charge-independent attractive force between nucleons that binds the nucleus; it becomes repulsive below about 0.8 fm.
Each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours, so the binding energy per nucleon does not grow with A over the middle range of the curve.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two medium-mass fragments with the release of neutrons and about 200 MeV of energy, e.g. neutron-induced fission of <sup>235</sup>U.
A self-sustaining sequence of fissions in which neutrons from one fission trigger further fissions; controlled in a reactor, uncontrolled in a bomb.
The joining of two light nuclei into a heavier one with the release of energy, e.g. four protons forming <sup>4</sup>He with 26.7 MeV in the Sun.
A fusion reaction that proceeds only at very high temperature, because the nuclei need enough kinetic energy to overcome their Coulomb repulsion.
A fully ionised gas of nuclei and free electrons, the state of fusion fuel at about 10<sup>8</sup> K; it must be confined by magnetic fields, not by a material vessel.

formula_sheet.name: Mass number
formula_sheet.note: Z protons, N neutrons; balance both Z and A in every nuclear equation.

formula_sheet.name: Atomic mass unit
formula_sheet.note: Multiply a mass difference in u by 931.5 to get MeV.

formula_sheet.name: Nucleon masses
formula_sheet.note: Use atomic masses (m(<sup>1</sup>H)) with atomic masses and nuclear masses (m<sub>p</sub>) with nuclear masses.

formula_sheet.name: Nuclear radius
formula_sheet.note: Volume ∝ A; radius ratio = cube root of mass-number ratio.

formula_sheet.name: Nuclear density
formula_sheet.note: Independent of A; about 10<sup>14</sup> times the density of water.

formula_sheet.name: Mass defect
formula_sheet.note: Always positive for a bound nucleus.

formula_sheet.name: Binding energy
formula_sheet.expr: E<sub>b</sub> = ΔM c<sup>2</sup> = ΔM (u) × 931.5 MeV; E<sub>bn</sub> = E<sub>b</sub>/A
formula_sheet.note: E<sub>bn</sub> ≈ 8 MeV for 30 < A < 170; 8.75 MeV at A = 56; 7.6 MeV at A = 238.

formula_sheet.name: Energy released in a reaction (Q value)
formula_sheet.expr: Q = [Σ m(reactants) − Σ m(products)] c<sup>2</sup> = Σ E<sub>b</sub>(products) − Σ E<sub>b</sub>(reactants)

formula_sheet.name: Fusion in the Sun (net)
formula_sheet.note: Proton-proton chain; core temperature about 1.5 × 10<sup>7</sup> K.

formula_sheet.name: Deuterium fusion reactions
formula_sheet.note: Candidate reactions for a fusion reactor at about 10<sup>8</sup> K.

formula_sheet.name: Coulomb barrier
formula_sheet.note: Two deuterons touching (r = 4 fm) give 360 keV; two protons about 400 keV; (3/2)kT ≈ U gives T ≈ 3 × 10<sup>9</sup> K.

diagrams.title: Binding energy per nucleon versus mass number
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes with A (0 to 250) on the x-axis and E<sub>bn</sub> in MeV (0 to 10) on the y-axis. Sketch a curve that rises steeply from hydrogen, shows a small sharp peak at <sup>4</sup>He, reaches a broad maximum of about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 (label <sup>56</sup>Fe), stays nearly flat around 8 MeV up to about A = 170, then falls gently to 7.6 MeV at <sup>238</sup>U. Mark the flat region 30 < A < 170 and the values 8.75 MeV and 7.6 MeV; add arrows showing fusion moving up the left side and fission moving from A ≈ 240 to A ≈ 120.

diagrams.title: Potential energy of a pair of nucleons versus their separation
diagrams.how_to_draw: Put separation r (fm) on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis with zero marked. Draw a curve that is large and positive at very small r (a steep repulsive wall), crosses zero, dips to a minimum at r<sub>0</sub> ≈ 0.8 fm, then rises back towards zero and stays at zero beyond about 3 fm. Label the region r > r<sub>0</sub> as attractive and r < r<sub>0</sub> as repulsive, and write r<sub>0</sub> = 0.8 fm at the minimum.

diagrams.title: Fission of uranium-235 and the chain reaction
diagrams.how_to_draw: Show a slow neutron entering a <sup>235</sup>U nucleus, the excited <sup>236</sup>U nucleus stretching into a dumb-bell, and then two fragments (label <sup>144</sup>Ba and <sup>89</sup>Kr) flying apart with three neutrons. For the chain reaction, let each emitted neutron strike another <sup>235</sup>U nucleus in the next row so that the number of fissions grows 1, 3, 9. Write Q ≈ 200 MeV beside the first fission.

diagrams.title: Proton-proton chain in the Sun
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw it as a flow: two pairs of protons each combine to give <sup>2</sup>H + e<sup>+</sup> + ν; each <sup>2</sup>H captures a proton to give <sup>3</sup>He + γ; the two <sup>3</sup>He nuclei combine to give <sup>4</sup>He and return two protons. Write the energy of each step (0.42, 5.49, 12.86 MeV, plus 1.02 MeV from each positron annihilation) and the net line 4 <sup>1</sup>H + 2e<sup>−</sup> → <sup>4</sup>He + 2ν + 6γ + 26.7 MeV underneath.

diagrams.title: Nuclear radius against A<sup>1/3</sup>
diagrams.how_to_draw: Plot A<sup>1/3</sup> on the x-axis and R (fm) on the y-axis. Draw a straight line through the origin with slope R<sub>0</sub> = 1.2 fm and mark a few nuclei, e.g. <sup>27</sup>Al at (3, 3.6) and <sup>64</sup>Cu at (4, 4.8). State that the linearity is what makes the nuclear density independent of A.

ncert_questions.q: Given the mass of iron nucleus as 55.85 u and A = 56, find the nuclear density.
ncert_questions.a:
Mass of nucleus m = 55.85 × 1.66 × 10−27 = 9.27 × 10−26 kg.

Volume = (4/3)πR3 = (4/3)π R03 A = (4/3) × 3.14 × (1.2 × 10−15)3 × 56 = 4.05 × 10−43 m3.

Density = 9.27 × 10−26 / 4.05 × 10−43 = 2.29 × 1017 kg m−3.

Nuclear matter is about 1014 times denser than water, and this value is the same for every nucleus.

ncert_questions.q: Calculate the energy equivalent of 1 g of substance.
ncert_questions.a:
E = mc2 = 10−3 kg × (3 × 108 m s−1)2 = 10−3 × 9 × 1016 = 9 × 1013 J.

This is the energy that would be released if 1 g of matter were converted entirely into energy; it shows why nuclear processes, which convert a small fraction of mass, release so much.

ncert_questions.q: Find the energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit, first in joules and then in MeV. Using this, express the mass defect of <sup>16</sup><sub>8</sub>O in MeV/c<sup>2</sup>.
ncert_questions.a:
1 u = 1.6605 × 10−27 kg. E = 1.6605 × 10−27 × (2.9979 × 108)2 = 1.4924 × 10−10 J.

In eV: 1.4924 × 10−10 / 1.602 × 10−19 = 0.9315 × 109 eV = 931.5 MeV. So 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c2.

For 16O, ΔM = 0.13691 u (from 8 mp + 8 mn − Mnucleus = 16.12744 − 15.99053), so ΔM = 0.13691 × 931.5 = 127.5 MeV/c2. The binding energy is 127.5 MeV, i.e. 7.97 MeV per nucleon.

ncert_questions.q: Obtain the binding energy (in MeV) of a nitrogen nucleus <sup>14</sup><sub>7</sub>N, given m(<sup>14</sup><sub>7</sub>N) = 14.00307 u.
ncert_questions.a:
Nitrogen-14 has 7 protons and 7 neutrons. Using atomic masses, m(1H) = 1.007825 u and mn = 1.008665 u:

ΔM = 7 × 1.007825 + 7 × 1.008665 − 14.00307 = 7.054775 + 7.060655 − 14.00307 = 0.11236 u.

Eb = 0.11236 × 931.5 = 104.66 MeV ≈ 104.7 MeV.

Binding energy per nucleon = 104.7/14 ≈ 7.48 MeV.

ncert_questions.q: Obtain the binding energy of the nuclei <sup>56</sup><sub>26</sub>Fe and <sup>209</sup><sub>83</sub>Bi in units of MeV from the following data: m(<sup>56</sup><sub>26</sub>Fe) = 55.934939 u, m(<sup>209</sup><sub>83</sub>Bi) = 208.980388 u.

A given coin has a mass of 3.0 g. Calculate the nuclear energy that would be required to separate all the neutrons and protons from each other. For simplicity assume that the coin is entirely made of <sup>63</sup><sub>29</sub>Cu atoms (of mass 62.92960 u).
Obtain approximately the ratio of the nuclear radii of the gold isotope <sup>197</sup><sub>79</sub>Au and the silver isotope <sup>107</sup><sub>47</sub>Ag.
ncert_questions.a:
R ∝ A1/3, so RAu/RAg = (197/107)1/3 = (1.841)1/3 ≈ 1.23.

Check: 1.233 = 1.86, close to 1.84. The gold nucleus is only about 23% larger in radius although it is nearly twice as massive, because volume, not radius, scales with A.

ncert_questions.q: The Q value of a nuclear reaction A + b → C + d is defined by Q = [m<sub>A</sub> + m<sub>b</sub> − m<sub>C</sub> − m<sub>d</sub>]c<sup>2</sup>, where the masses refer to the respective nuclei. Determine from the given data the Q-value of the following reactions and state whether the reactions are exothermic or endothermic. (i) <sup>1</sup><sub>1</sub>H + <sup>3</sup><sub>1</sub>H → <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H + <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H (ii) <sup>12</sup><sub>6</sub>C + <sup>12</sup><sub>6</sub>C → <sup>20</sup><sub>10</sub>Ne + <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He. Atomic masses: m(<sup>1</sup>H) = 1.007825 u, m(<sup>2</sup>H) = 2.014102 u, m(<sup>3</sup>H) = 3.016049 u, m(<sup>12</sup>C) = 12.000000 u, m(<sup>20</sup>Ne) = 19.992439 u, m(<sup>4</sup>He) = 4.002603 u.
ncert_questions.a:
Electron masses are equal on both sides, so atomic masses can be used directly.

(i) Q = [1.007825 + 3.016049 − 2 × 2.014102] × 931.5 = [4.023874 − 4.028204] × 931.5 = (−0.004330) × 931.5 = −4.03 MeV. Q is negative: the reaction is endothermic; 4.03 MeV must be supplied as kinetic energy of the reactants.

(ii) Q = [2 × 12.000000 − 19.992439 − 4.002603] × 931.5 = [24.000000 − 23.995042] × 931.5 = 0.004958 × 931.5 = 4.62 MeV. Q is positive: the reaction is exothermic, releasing 4.62 MeV.

ncert_questions.q: Suppose we think of fission of a <sup>56</sup><sub>26</sub>Fe nucleus into two equal fragments <sup>28</sup><sub>13</sub>Al. Is the fission energetically possible? Argue by working out Q of the process. Given m(<sup>56</sup><sub>26</sub>Fe) = 55.93494 u and m(<sup>28</sup><sub>13</sub>Al) = 27.98191 u.
ncert_questions.a:
Q = [m(56Fe) − 2 m(28Al)] × 931.5 = [55.93494 − 2 × 27.98191] × 931.5 = [55.93494 − 55.96382] × 931.5 = (−0.02888) × 931.5 = −26.90 MeV.

Q is negative, so the fission is not energetically possible: about 26.9 MeV would have to be supplied. This agrees with the binding-energy curve: iron sits at the maximum of Ebn, so splitting it produces fragments that are less tightly bound, not more.

ncert_questions.q: The fission properties of <sup>239</sup><sub>94</sub>Pu are very similar to those of <sup>235</sup><sub>92</sub>U. The average energy released per fission is 180 MeV. How much energy, in MeV, is released if all the atoms in 1 kg of pure <sup>239</sup><sub>94</sub>Pu undergo fission?

How long can an electric lamp of 100 W be kept glowing by fusion of 2.0 kg of deuterium? Take the fusion reaction as <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H + <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H → <sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>He + n + 3.27 MeV.
ncert_questions.a:
Number of deuterium atoms in 2.0 kg = (2000/2) × 6.023 × 1023 = 6.023 × 1026.

Each reaction uses 2 atoms and releases 3.27 MeV, so total energy = (6.023 × 1026/2) × 3.27 = 9.848 × 1026 MeV = 9.848 × 1026 × 1.6 × 10−13 J = 1.576 × 1014 J.

Time = energy/power = 1.576 × 1014/100 = 1.576 × 1012 s.

In years: 1.576 × 1012 / (3.156 × 107) ≈ 4.9 × 104 years. The lamp would glow for about fifty thousand years.

ncert_questions.q: Calculate the height of the potential barrier for a head-on collision of two deuterons. (Hint: the height of the potential barrier is given by the Coulomb repulsion between the two deuterons when they just touch each other. Assume that they can be taken as hard spheres of radius 2.0 fm.)
ncert_questions.a:
When the deuterons just touch, the distance between their centres is r = 2 × 2.0 fm = 4.0 × 10−15 m.

Potential energy U = (1/4πε0) e2/r = 9 × 109 × (1.6 × 10−19)2 / 4.0 × 10−15 = 9 × 109 × 2.56 × 10−38 / 4.0 × 10−15 = 5.76 × 10−14 J.

In eV: 5.76 × 10−14 / 1.6 × 10−19 = 3.6 × 105 eV = 360 keV.

The barrier height is 360 keV; each deuteron must bring about 180 keV of kinetic energy in a head-on collision, which is why fusion needs temperatures of the order of 109 K.

ncert_questions.q: From the relation R = R<sub>0</sub>A<sup>1/3</sup>, where R<sub>0</sub> is a constant and A is the mass number of a nucleus, show that the nuclear matter density is nearly constant (i.e. independent of A).
ncert_questions.a:
Mass of the nucleus ≈ A m, where m is the mass of one nucleon.

Volume of the nucleus = (4/3)πR3 = (4/3)π(R0A1/3)3 = (4/3)πR03A.

Density ρ = mass/volume = A m / [(4/3)πR03A] = 3m/(4πR03).

A cancels, so ρ depends only on the constants m and R0 and is the same for all nuclei. Numerically ρ ≈ 3 × 1.67 × 10−27 / [4π × (1.2 × 10−15)3] ≈ 2.3 × 1017 kg m−3.

pyq.q: Two nuclei have mass numbers in the ratio 1 : 8. The ratio of their nuclear radii is
pyq.answer: c

pyq.q: The density of nuclear matter
options: is independent of mass number A
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Mass ∝ A and volume ∝ R<sup>3</sup> ∝ A, so their ratio is a constant, about 2.3 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup> for every nucleus.

pyq.q: The energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit is approximately
pyq.answer: c

pyq.q: The binding energy per nucleon is maximum for
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The binding-energy curve peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56; helium has a local peak of about 7.07 MeV, uranium has 7.6 MeV, and hydrogen-1 has no binding energy at all.

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about the nuclear force is not correct?
options: It varies inversely as the square of the distance between nucleons
It is much stronger than the Coulomb force
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The nuclear force has no simple inverse-square form; it falls off to zero within a few femtometres. The other three are standard properties.

pyq.q: The energy released in the fission of one <sup>235</sup>U nucleus is of the order of
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The fragments have about 0.9 MeV per nucleon more binding energy than uranium; 0.9 × 236 ≈ 200 MeV.

pyq.q: The source of energy of the Sun is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In the proton-proton chain four protons form one helium-4 nucleus, releasing 26.7 MeV; the Sun's core temperature of about 1.5 × 10<sup>7</sup> K makes this thermonuclear reaction possible.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The nuclear density is the same for all nuclei. Reason (R): The radius of a nucleus is proportional to A<sup>1/3</sup>, so its volume is proportional to its mass number.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Mass ∝ A and volume ∝ A, so density = mass/volume is independent of A. R is exactly why A is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Energy is released when a heavy nucleus such as <sup>235</sup>U undergoes fission. Reason (R): The binding energy per nucleon of the fission fragments is greater than that of the parent nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The fragments (A ≈ 120, E<sub>bn</sub> ≈ 8.5 MeV) are more tightly bound than uranium (E<sub>bn</sub> ≈ 7.6 MeV); the difference in total binding energy, about 200 MeV, is released.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant, about 8 MeV, for nuclei with 30 < A < 170. Reason (R): The nuclear force is a long-range force acting between all pairs of nucleons in the nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is a correct feature of the curve. R is false: the nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates, which is precisely why E<sub>bn</sub> stays constant instead of growing with A.

pyq.q: The nuclear radius of <sup>27</sup><sub>13</sub>Al is 3.6 fermi. Find the nuclear radius of <sup>64</sup><sub>29</sub>Cu.
pyq.answer:
R = R0A1/3, so RCu/RAl = (ACu/AAl)1/3 = (64/27)1/3 = 4/3.

RCu = 3.6 × 4/3 = 4.8 fermi.

pyq.q: Four nuclei of an element undergo fusion to form a heavier nucleus, with release of energy. Which of the two, the parent or the daughter nucleus, would have higher binding energy per nucleon?
pyq.answer:
The daughter nucleus. Energy is released in a nuclear reaction only when the products are more tightly bound than the reactants, i.e. when the total binding energy increases.

Fusion of light nuclei moves the system up the steep left side of the Ebn versus A curve, so the heavier daughter nucleus has a higher binding energy per nucleon than the parent nuclei, and the difference appears as the released energy.

pyq.q: Define mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus. How are they related?
pyq.answer:
Mass defect is the difference between the sum of the masses of the free nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus: ΔM = [Z mp + (A − Z) mn] − M.

Binding energy is the energy needed to break a nucleus into its constituent nucleons (equivalently, the energy released when they come together to form the nucleus).

Relation: Eb = ΔM c2; with ΔM in u, Eb = ΔM × 931.5 MeV.

pyq.q: State two characteristic properties of the nuclear force that distinguish it from the Coulomb force.
pyq.answer:
(i) It is short-ranged: it acts only over a few femtometres and becomes negligible beyond that, whereas the Coulomb force is long-ranged (1/r2).

(ii) It is charge independent: the n–n, p–p and n–p forces are nearly equal, whereas the Coulomb force acts only between charged particles.

(Any two; also acceptable: it is much stronger than the Coulomb force; it saturates; it becomes repulsive below about 0.8 fm.)

pyq.q: Calculate the energy released in the fusion reaction <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H + <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H → <sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>He + n, given that the binding energy of <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H is 2.23 MeV and of <sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>He is 7.73 MeV.
pyq.answer:
Energy released = total binding energy of products − total binding energy of reactants.

Products: Eb(3He) = 7.73 MeV; the free neutron has no binding energy. Reactants: 2 × Eb(2H) = 2 × 2.23 = 4.46 MeV.

Energy released = 7.73 − 4.46 = 3.27 MeV.

pyq.q: Using the relation R = R<sub>0</sub>A<sup>1/3</sup>, show that the density of a nucleus is independent of its mass number A. Estimate its value.
pyq.answer:
Let m be the average mass of a nucleon. Mass of the nucleus M ≈ A m.

Volume V = (4/3)πR3 = (4/3)π(R0A1/3)3 = (4/3)πR03A.

Density ρ = M/V = A m / [(4/3)πR03A] = 3m/(4πR03).

Since A cancels, the density is independent of the mass number and is the same for all nuclei.

Value: ρ = 3 × 1.67 × 10−27 / [4 × 3.14 × (1.2 × 10−15)3] = 5.01 × 10−27 / 2.17 × 10−44 ≈ 2.3 × 1017 kg m−3.

pyq.q: Draw a plot of the potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Mark the regions where the nuclear force is (i) attractive and (ii) repulsive. Write any two characteristic features of nuclear forces.
pyq.answer:
Plot: potential energy U on the y-axis against separation r on the x-axis. The curve is large and positive at very small r (steep repulsive wall), crosses zero, reaches a minimum at r0 ≈ 0.8 fm, then rises back to zero and stays there beyond a few fm.

(i) Attractive region: r > r0 (about 0.8 fm), where U decreases as the nucleons approach. (ii) Repulsive region: r < r0, where U rises steeply.

Features: (1) The nuclear force is short-ranged, falling to zero beyond a few femtometres, so it saturates and each nucleon interacts only with its neighbours. (2) It is charge independent: the n–n, p–p and n–p forces are nearly equal. (Also acceptable: it is the strongest known force, far stronger than the Coulomb force.)

pyq.q: A heavy nucleus of mass number A = 240 and binding energy per nucleon 7.6 MeV splits into two fragments each of mass number 120 with binding energy per nucleon 8.5 MeV. Calculate the energy released in the process.
pyq.answer:
Total binding energy of the parent = 240 × 7.6 = 1824 MeV.

Total binding energy of the two fragments = 2 × 120 × 8.5 = 2040 MeV.

Energy released = binding energy of products − binding energy of reactants = 2040 − 1824 = 216 MeV.

The fragments are more tightly bound than the parent, so the reaction is exothermic; this is the origin of fission energy.

pyq.q: Calculate the binding energy and the binding energy per nucleon of a <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He nucleus. Given m(<sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He) = 4.002603 u, m(<sup>1</sup><sub>1</sub>H) = 1.007825 u, m<sub>n</sub> = 1.008665 u and 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c<sup>2</sup>.
pyq.answer:
Helium-4 has Z = 2, N = 2. Using atomic masses (electron masses cancel):

ΔM = 2 × 1.007825 + 2 × 1.008665 − 4.002603 = 2.015650 + 2.017330 − 4.002603 = 0.030377 u.

Eb = 0.030377 × 931.5 = 28.30 MeV.

Ebn = 28.30/4 = 7.07 MeV per nucleon.

This is unusually high for such a light nucleus, which is why 4He appears as a sharp peak on the binding-energy curve and why alpha particles are so stable.

pyq.q: Draw a plot of the binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number for a large number of nuclei. Write the main features of the plot and explain, using it, the release of energy in the processes of nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
pyq.answer:
Plot: Ebn (MeV) on the y-axis, mass number A on the x-axis. The curve rises steeply for light nuclei with a small sharp peak at 4He, reaches a broad maximum of about 8.75 MeV at A = 56 (56Fe), stays almost flat near 8 MeV up to about A = 170, and then falls slowly to 7.6 MeV at 238U.

Features: (i) Ebn is practically constant (≈ 8 MeV) for 30 < A < 170, showing that the nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates: each nucleon is bound only to its near neighbours, so adding nucleons does not change the energy per nucleon. (ii) The maximum near A = 56 makes iron-group nuclei the most stable. (iii) Ebn is lower for light nuclei (A < 30) because a large fraction of their nucleons sit on the surface with fewer neighbours, and lower for heavy nuclei (A > 170) because the long-range Coulomb repulsion between the many protons reduces the binding.

Fission: A heavy nucleus such as A = 240 (Ebn ≈ 7.6 MeV) splits into two fragments of A ≈ 120 (Ebn ≈ 8.5 MeV). The fragments are more tightly bound, so the total binding energy increases by about 0.9 MeV per nucleon, roughly 200 MeV in all, and this is released as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons.

Fusion: Two very light nuclei (A ≤ 10) on the steep left side of the curve join to form a heavier nucleus with a larger Ebn. Again the product is more tightly bound than the reactants, and the increase in binding energy is released, e.g. 4 1H → 4He + 26.7 MeV in the Sun.

In both processes the rule is the same: energy is released whenever the products lie higher on the curve than the reactants.

pyq.q: (a) Explain, with the help of the proton-proton chain, how energy is generated in the Sun. Write the net reaction and the energy released. (b) Why does nuclear fusion require a very high temperature? Why is the actual temperature of the Sun's core lower than the value estimated from the Coulomb barrier?
pyq.answer:
(a) In the Sun's core hydrogen is converted to helium in the proton-proton chain:

11H + 11H → 21H + e+ + ν + 0.42 MeV
e+ + e− → γ + γ + 1.02 MeV
21H + 11H → 32He + γ + 5.49 MeV
32He + 32He → 42He + 11H + 11H + 12.86 MeV

The first three steps occur twice for each occurrence of the last. Net reaction: 4 11H + 2e− → 42He + 2ν + 6γ + 26.7 MeV. Four hydrogen atoms become one helium atom with the release of 26.7 MeV; the helium nucleus has a higher binding energy per nucleon than the protons, and the difference is the energy released.

(b) For two nuclei to fuse they must come within a few fm so that the short-range nuclear force can act, but until then their positive charges repel. For two protons the Coulomb barrier is about 400 keV. Only at very high temperature do nuclei have enough thermal kinetic energy to cross it: setting (3/2)kT ≈ 400 keV gives T ≈ 3 × 109 K. Hence fusion is a thermonuclear reaction.

The Sun's core is at only about 1.5 × 107 K, yet fusion proceeds, because at any temperature the particles have a distribution of speeds and a fraction of them carry energies well above the average; those in the high-energy tail are the ones that fuse. The extreme density and pressure of the core also help. The fusion rate is slow, which is why the Sun has burnt hydrogen for about 5 × 109 years and will continue for about as long again.

pyq.q: (a) Write three characteristic properties of the nuclear force. (b) Explain why the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant for nuclei with 30 < A < 170. (c) Calculate the energy released, in joules, when 1 kg of <sup>235</sup>U undergoes complete fission, taking the energy released per fission as 200 MeV. (Avogadro number = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10<sup>−13</sup> J.)
pyq.answer:
(a) (i) The nuclear force is the strongest known force, much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion between protons. (ii) It is short-ranged: it acts only over a few femtometres and saturates, so each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours; the potential energy of a nucleon pair has a minimum at r0 ≈ 0.8 fm, the force being attractive for r > r0 and repulsive for r < r0. (iii) It is charge independent: the n–n, p–p and n–p forces are nearly equal.

(b) Because the force saturates, a nucleon in the interior of any nucleus is bound to roughly the same number of neighbours regardless of how big the nucleus is. Adding more nucleons adds binding energy in proportion to A, so Eb/A stays roughly constant at about 8 MeV. (For A > 170 the long-range Coulomb repulsion between protons, which does not saturate, slowly lowers Ebn; for A < 30 too many nucleons are on the surface with fewer neighbours.)

(c) Number of nuclei in 1 kg = (1000/235) × 6.022 × 1023 = 2.563 × 1024.

Energy = 2.563 × 1024 × 200 MeV = 5.126 × 1026 MeV = 5.126 × 1026 × 1.6 × 10−13 J ≈ 8.2 × 1013 J.

pyq.q:
The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy needed to separate it into its constituent nucleons; it equals the mass defect times c2. When the binding energy per nucleon Ebn is plotted against mass number A, the curve rises steeply for light nuclei, reaches a broad maximum of about 8.75 MeV near A = 56, stays nearly flat at about 8 MeV up to A ≈ 170, and then falls slowly to 7.6 MeV for uranium. Nuclei near the middle of the curve are the most stable. Energy is released in any nuclear process in which the products lie higher on the curve than the reactants.
(i) Which nucleus has the highest binding energy per nucleon: 4He, 56Fe, 120Sn or 238U?
(ii) A nucleus has mass defect 0.2 u. What is its binding energy in MeV?
(iii) Why does Ebn decrease for A > 170?
(iv) Fission of 56Fe into two 28Al nuclei has Q = −26.9 MeV. What does the negative sign tell you?
pyq.answer:
(i) 56Fe, at the peak of the curve (about 8.75 MeV per nucleon).

(ii) Eb = 0.2 × 931.5 = 186.3 MeV.

(iii) The nuclear force saturates, so its contribution per nucleon stops growing, but the Coulomb repulsion between protons is long-ranged and grows with the number of proton pairs; in heavy nuclei it reduces the net binding per nucleon.

(iv) The products are less tightly bound than iron, so energy would have to be supplied, not released; the fission of iron is not energetically possible on its own.

pyq.q:
In the Sun's core, at a temperature of about 1.5 × 107 K, hydrogen is converted into helium through the proton-proton chain. The net result is that four protons form one helium-4 nucleus, two positrons and two neutrinos, with the release of 26.7 MeV. To fuse, two nuclei must approach within a few femtometres against their Coulomb repulsion; the barrier for two protons is about 400 keV, so a very high temperature is required and the reaction is called thermonuclear. On Earth, a fusion reactor would use deuterium and tritium, 2H + 3H → 4He + n + 17.59 MeV, at about 108 K, where the fuel is a plasma that must be held away from the walls by magnetic fields.
(i) Why is fusion called a thermonuclear reaction?
(ii) How many positrons are produced when one helium-4 nucleus is formed in the proton-proton chain?
(iii) Why can the plasma in a fusion reactor not be held in an ordinary metal container?
(iv) State one advantage of fusion over fission as a source of energy.
pyq.answer:
(i) Because it occurs only at extremely high temperature: the nuclei need large thermal kinetic energy to overcome their Coulomb repulsion and come within the range of the nuclear force.

(ii) Two. Each of the two 1H + 1H → 2H steps releases one positron.

(iii) At about 108 K the fuel is a fully ionised plasma; contact with a wall would cool the plasma below fusion temperature and melt or vaporise the wall. It is therefore confined by magnetic fields.

(iv) The fuel (deuterium from water) is practically unlimited, and the products are not long-lived radioactive fragments; also more energy is released per unit mass of fuel than in fission.

common_mistakes: Taking R ∝ A instead of A<sup>1/3</sup>. A nucleus with eight times the mass number has only twice the radius; examiners set ratios like 1 : 8 and 27 : 64 precisely to catch this.
Claiming nuclear density depends on A. Mass and volume are both proportional to A, so the density is the same for every nucleus; the derivation must show A cancelling.

Mixing atomic and nuclear masses in a mass-defect calculation. Use Z m(<sup>1</sup>H) with atomic masses or Z m<sub>p</sub> with nuclear masses; subtracting electrons on one side only gives a wrong answer that no rounding will rescue.

Getting the sign of the energy backwards. Energy released = binding energy of products − binding energy of reactants (or mass of reactants − mass of products, times c<sup>2</sup>). A positive Q means energy is released.

Saying that energy is released in fission because 'mass is converted to energy' and stopping there. The examiner wants the curve: the fragments have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the parent, so they are more tightly bound and the difference is released.

Drawing the binding-energy curve as a smooth hump with no numbers. Mark 8.75 MeV at A = 56, 7.6 MeV at A = 238, the flat region 30 to 170, and label both axes with units, or the diagram marks are lost.
Drawing the nucleon potential-energy curve as a simple well without the steep repulsive wall at r < 0.8 fm, and forgetting to label r<sub>0</sub> and the attractive and repulsive regions.

Answering 'why does fusion need high temperature' with only 'to provide activation energy'. State the physics: positive nuclei must overcome Coulomb repulsion to come within a few fm, the range of the nuclear force.
Spending revision time on half-life, decay constant and the nuclear reactor. These were removed from the CBSE syllabus in 2023-24 and are not asked in the current pattern.
strategy:
Nuclei is one of the shortest chapters in the syllabus and one of the most predictable. Budget about three hours in total and aim for full marks.

Hour one: the two graphs. Draw the binding energy per nucleon curve five times from memory until the numbers come without thinking: 8.75 MeV at Fe-56, 7.6 MeV at U-238, flat near 8 MeV between A = 30 and 170. Beside it write the four conclusions (attractive force, saturation and short range, fission from the right, fusion from the left). Then draw the nucleon potential-energy curve with its repulsive wall, the minimum at 0.8 fm, and the two labelled regions. Between them these two sketches answer the 3-mark and 5-mark questions in nearly every paper.

Hour two: the numericals. There are only four kinds. Radius ratios from R = R0A1/3 (look for perfect cubes). The density derivation, written as three separate lines. Mass defect to binding energy, using 931.5 MeV per u and the right kind of masses. Energy released from binding energies per nucleon or from a Q value. Work NCERT exercises 13.1 to 13.10 once each; they are the templates.

Hour three: the words. Learn the definitions of mass defect, binding energy, isotope, isobar and isotone; the five properties of the nuclear force; the fission equation with Q ≈ 200 MeV; the proton-proton chain and its net line with 26.7 MeV; and the two-sentence answer to why fusion needs a high temperature. Finish with the practice MCQs and the two case studies.

In the exam, answer the numerical from this chapter early: it is short, mechanical and full-credit if the units and the 931.5 conversion are shown. Do not write about radioactivity or reactors; they are out of the syllabus and earn nothing.
revision_checklist: I can define u and state 1 u = 1.660539 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg = 931.5 MeV/c<sup>2</sup>.
I can write Chadwick's reaction for the discovery of the neutron and give m<sub>p</sub> and m<sub>n</sub> in u.
I can distinguish isotopes, isobars and isotones with one example each.
I can write R = R<sub>0</sub>A<sup>1/3</sup> with R<sub>0</sub> = 1.2 fm and find a radius ratio from a mass-number ratio in one line.
I can derive in three lines that nuclear density is independent of A and quote 2.3 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>.
I can define mass defect and binding energy, write ΔM = [Z m<sub>p</sub> + (A − Z) m<sub>n</sub>] − M and E<sub>b</sub> = ΔM c<sup>2</sup>.
I can compute the binding energy of a nucleus from given atomic masses without mixing in electron masses.
I can draw the E<sub>bn</sub> versus A curve with 8.75 MeV at A = 56, 7.6 MeV at A = 238 and the flat region 30 to 170 marked.
I can state the four conclusions from the curve and explain both fission and fusion from it.
I can list five properties of the nuclear force and draw the nucleon potential-energy curve with r<sub>0</sub> = 0.8 fm.
I can write the fission equation of <sup>235</sup>U with balanced Z and A and quote Q ≈ 200 MeV.
I can compute the energy from 1 kg of fissile material given the energy per fission.
I can write the proton-proton chain, its net reaction and 26.7 MeV, and explain why fusion needs about 10<sup>7</sup> K.
I can compute energy released in a reaction from binding energies (e.g. 7.73 − 2 × 2.23 = 3.27 MeV) or from a Q value.
I know that radioactivity, half-life and the nuclear reactor are no longer in the syllabus and will not spend exam time on them.
